title: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease

cards.explanation: Two viruses infecting humans need not affect the same tissues or produce the same clinical course.
cards.text: Differences in viral target cells, replication, immune responses and persistence help explain different {{c1::patterns of disease}}.
cards.question: Differences in viral target cells, replication, immune responses and persistence help explain different {{c1::patterns of disease}}.

cards.explanation: Influenza is the lecture’s example. Acute describes the course; it does not mean every case is mild or invariably clears without complications.
cards.text: Symptoms followed by viral clearance in many cases describe an {{c1::acute infection}}.
cards.question: Symptoms followed by viral clearance in many cases describe an {{c1::acute infection}}.

cards.explanation: HSV and VZV illustrate persistence between symptomatic episodes, rather than continuous symptomatic disease.
cards.text: A persisting viral genome with episodes of reactivation describes {{c1::latent infection}}.
cards.question: A persisting viral genome with episodes of reactivation describes {{c1::latent infection}}.

cards.explanation: HIV is the example. Persistent infection and latency are related concepts but not interchangeable clinical patterns.
cards.text: An infection continuing over time with ongoing or intermittent activity is {{c1::chronic or persistent}}.
cards.question: An infection continuing over time with ongoing or intermittent activity is {{c1::chronic or persistent}}.

cards.explanation: Potential means increased cancer risk, not inevitable malignant transformation.
cards.text: Persistent high-risk HPV illustrates a viral infection with {{c1::oncogenic potential}}.
cards.question: Persistent high-risk HPV illustrates a viral infection with {{c1::oncogenic potential}}.

cards.explanation: The latent viral genome persists after an episode of epithelial disease resolves.
cards.text: HSV-1 and HSV-2 establish latency in {{c1::sensory neurons}}.
cards.question: HSV-1 and HSV-2 establish latency in {{c1::sensory neurons}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture groups HSV-1 and HSV-2 together; it does not claim that either type is restricted exclusively to one anatomical site.
cards.text: Typical symptomatic HSV infection produces oral or genital {{c1::lesions}}.
cards.question: Typical symptomatic HSV infection produces oral or genital {{c1::lesions}}.

cards.explanation: This differs from the reactivation disease caused by the same virus.
cards.text: Primary varicella-zoster virus infection causes {{c1::chickenpox}}.
cards.question: Primary varicella-zoster virus infection causes {{c1::chickenpox}}.

cards.explanation: Chickenpox and shingles are different stages of infection with the same virus, not infections with two separate viruses.
cards.text: Reactivation of latent VZV causes {{c1::shingles}}.
cards.question: Reactivation of latent VZV causes {{c1::shingles}}.

cards.explanation: A ganglion contains neuronal cell bodies; the lecture links this reservoir with later reactivation.
cards.text: VZV persists latently in {{c1::sensory ganglia}}.
cards.question: VZV persists latently in {{c1::sensory ganglia}}.

cards.explanation: This is consistent with reactivation from a sensory ganglion. The lecture says often, not that every case is strictly limited to one dermatome.
cards.text: Shingles often follows the skin distribution of a {{c1::dermatome}}.
cards.question: Shingles often follows the skin distribution of a {{c1::dermatome}}.

cards.explanation: Loss of effective control can allow the latent virus to reactivate.
cards.text: Latent VZV is usually kept under control by {{c1::immune surveillance}}.
cards.question: Latent VZV is usually kept under control by {{c1::immune surveillance}}.

cards.explanation: A weakened ability to control latent infection increases the likelihood of shingles.
cards.text: VZV reactivation becomes more likely with age or {{c1::impaired immunity}}.
cards.question: VZV reactivation becomes more likely with age or {{c1::impaired immunity}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture separates direct viral injury from additional injury associated with the host response.
cards.text: HSV/VZV replication directly damages infected {{c1::epithelial cells}}.
cards.question: HSV/VZV replication directly damages infected {{c1::epithelial cells}}.

cards.explanation: Symptoms reflect both infected-cell damage and the immune response, not viral replication alone.
cards.text: Host {{c1::inflammation}} contributes to the pain, redness and lesions of HSV/VZV disease.
cards.question: Host {{c1::inflammation}} contributes to the pain, redness and lesions of HSV/VZV disease.

cards.explanation: They reduce viral replication during active disease while the latent genome remains in neurons.
cards.text: Treating a cold sore does not permanently remove HSV because antivirals do not eliminate {{c1::latency}}.
cards.question: Treating a cold sore does not permanently remove HSV because antivirals do not eliminate {{c1::latency}}.

cards.explanation: Close contact can favour transmission. The lecture does not describe it as exclusively spread by contaminated objects.
cards.text: Influenza is transmitted primarily through virus-containing {{c1::respiratory particles}}.
cards.question: Influenza is transmitted primarily through virus-containing {{c1::respiratory particles}}.

cards.explanation: Infection of these cells contributes to the respiratory disease pattern.
cards.text: The main target tissue identified for influenza is the {{c1::respiratory epithelium}}.
cards.question: The main target tissue identified for influenza is the {{c1::respiratory epithelium}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture links these contributions with fever, cough and malaise. Symptoms cannot be attributed only to direct viral damage.
cards.text: Influenza severity reflects viral infection together with the {{c1::host immune response}}.
cards.question: Influenza severity reflects viral infection together with the {{c1::host immune response}}.

cards.explanation: Changes in surface antigens can reduce recognition by existing antibodies.
cards.text: Gradual accumulation of mutations affecting influenza antigens is {{c1::antigenic drift}}.
cards.question: Gradual accumulation of mutations affecting influenza antigens is {{c1::antigenic drift}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture associates shift with the potential emergence of pandemic strains; a new combination does not guarantee a pandemic.
cards.text: Abrupt emergence of a novel influenza A antigenic combination is {{c1::antigenic shift}}.
cards.question: Abrupt emergence of a novel influenza A antigenic combination is {{c1::antigenic shift}}.

cards.explanation: Reassortment reshuffles genome segments, unlike gradual mutation accumulation in drift.
cards.text: Influenza antigenic shift often involves genome {{c1::reassortment}}.
cards.question: Influenza antigenic shift often involves genome {{c1::reassortment}}.

cards.explanation: Shift is instead the abrupt-change concept highlighted for potentially pandemic influenza A strains.
cards.text: The gradual antigenic process helping explain seasonal vaccine updates is {{c1::drift}}.
cards.question: The gradual antigenic process helping explain seasonal vaccine updates is {{c1::drift}}.

cards.explanation: This helps explain repeated review and updating of vaccine composition.
cards.text: Influenza evolution can reduce how well existing {{c1::antibodies recognise circulating viruses}}.
cards.question: Influenza evolution can reduce how well existing {{c1::antibodies recognise circulating viruses}}.

cards.explanation: A poor match can reduce protection; vaccine composition is not assumed to stay equally effective indefinitely.
cards.text: Influenza vaccine composition is reviewed to match {{c1::circulating strains}}.
cards.question: Influenza vaccine composition is reviewed to match {{c1::circulating strains}}.

cards.explanation: Protection varies between individuals; vaccination is not a guarantee that infection cannot occur.
cards.text: Besides strain match, age and {{c1::immune status}} can influence protection from influenza vaccination.
cards.question: Besides strain match, age and {{c1::immune status}} can influence protection from influenza vaccination.

cards.explanation: Prevention of infection and reduction in severity are different outcomes.
cards.text: Influenza vaccination can reduce severe disease even when it does not completely {{c1::prevent infection}}.
cards.question: Influenza vaccination can reduce severe disease even when it does not completely {{c1::prevent infection}}.

cards.explanation: These include CD4 T lymphocytes; the wording does not restrict all HIV targets to T cells alone.
cards.text: HIV primarily infects {{c1::CD4-expressing immune cells}}.
cards.question: HIV primarily infects {{c1::CD4-expressing immune cells}}.

cards.explanation: This allows viral genetic material to remain within infected cells rather than merely being present outside them.
cards.text: HIV persistence involves reverse transcription followed by {{c1::integration}} of viral genetic material into host cells.
cards.question: HIV persistence involves reverse transcription followed by {{c1::integration}} of viral genetic material into host cells.

cards.explanation: Progressive immune damage reduces the host’s ability to control infections that take advantage of impaired immunity.
cards.text: Untreated HIV increases susceptibility to {{c1::opportunistic infections}}.
cards.question: Untreated HIV increases susceptibility to {{c1::opportunistic infections}}.

cards.explanation: HIV names the virus; AIDS names a clinical stage. Having HIV is not the same as already having AIDS.
cards.text: AIDS is an advanced clinical stage of {{c1::HIV infection}}.
cards.question: AIDS is an advanced clinical stage of {{c1::HIV infection}}.

cards.explanation: This helps explain susceptibility to opportunistic disease when infection is untreated.
cards.text: Loss of CD4 T cells contributes to HIV-associated {{c1::immune dysfunction}}.
cards.question: Loss of CD4 T cells contributes to HIV-associated {{c1::immune dysfunction}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture describes suppression and long-term health, not eradication of all persistent viral genetic material.
cards.text: Combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) {{c1::suppresses viral replication}}.
cards.question: Combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) {{c1::suppresses viral replication}}.

cards.explanation: This is the lecture’s undetectable-equals-untransmittable principle. It concerns sustained effective treatment and sexual transmission; undetectable does not mean cured or cover every possible route.
cards.text: Effective ART prevents {{c1::sexual transmission}} when viral load remains undetectable.
cards.question: Effective ART prevents {{c1::sexual transmission}} when viral load remains undetectable.

cards.explanation: The lecture explicitly distinguishes this common outcome from persistent high-risk infection.
cards.text: Many HPV infections are controlled and cleared by the {{c1::immune system}}.
cards.question: Many HPV infections are controlled and cleared by the {{c1::immune system}}.

cards.explanation: This can contribute to precancerous changes. The slides do not specify molecular protein targets, so these are not invented.
cards.text: Persistent high-risk HPV can disrupt normal {{c1::cell-cycle control}}.
cards.question: Persistent high-risk HPV can disrupt normal {{c1::cell-cycle control}}.

cards.explanation: The result identifies infection or its evidence in the relevant testing context, not a cancer diagnosis. Persistence and subsequent changes matter.
cards.text: A positive high-risk HPV test does {{c1::not mean a person has cancer}}.
cards.question: A positive high-risk HPV test does {{c1::not mean a person has cancer}}.
cards.answer: not mean a person has cancer

cards.explanation: The diagram shows a branching outcome, not inevitable progression to precancer and cancer.
cards.text: After HPV infection, immune clearance is an alternative to {{c1::persistence}}.
cards.question: After HPV infection, immune clearance is an alternative to {{c1::persistence}}.

cards.explanation: The pathway is possible rather than inevitable; the slide gives no numerical individual cancer-risk estimate.
cards.text: Cancer develops in only a {{c1::minority}} of persistent high-risk HPV infections.
cards.question: Cancer develops in only a {{c1::minority}} of persistent high-risk HPV infections.

cards.explanation: They serve different preventive roles. The lecture does not suggest that vaccination makes screening unnecessary.
cards.text: HPV vaccination and cervical screening are {{c1::complementary}} prevention strategies.
cards.question: HPV vaccination and cervical screening are {{c1::complementary}} prevention strategies.

cards.explanation: The comparison table links different viral biology with different clinical outcomes.
cards.text: Recurrent lesions or shingles chiefly illustrate {{c1::latency and reactivation}}, rather than the acute influenza pattern.
cards.question: Recurrent lesions or shingles chiefly illustrate {{c1::latency and reactivation}}, rather than the acute influenza pattern.

cards.explanation: The table contrasts opportunistic infection risk with increased risk of certain cancers; persistence does not produce the same outcome for every virus.
cards.text: Untreated HIV and persistent high-risk HPV differ in emphasis: HIV causes immune dysfunction, while HPV can alter {{c1::cell-cycle control}}.
cards.question: Untreated HIV and persistent high-risk HPV differ in emphasis: HIV causes immune dysfunction, while HPV can alter {{c1::cell-cycle control}}.

cards.explanation: These help form a differential diagnosis before or alongside laboratory investigation.
cards.text: Clinical interpretation of suspected viral infection uses symptoms, timing, examination and {{c1::exposure history}}.
cards.question: Clinical interpretation of suspected viral infection uses symptoms, timing, examination and {{c1::exposure history}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture lists it alongside antigen testing and serology as a laboratory approach.
cards.text: PCR is an example of a {{c1::nucleic acid amplification test}}.
cards.question: PCR is an example of a {{c1::nucleic acid amplification test}}.

cards.explanation: PCR, antigen tests and serology are not interchangeable in every phase of infection; the slides do not provide virus-specific testing windows.
cards.text: The diagnostic question and timing help determine the appropriate {{c1::laboratory test}}.
cards.question: The diagnostic question and timing help determine the appropriate {{c1::laboratory test}}.

cards.explanation: Symptoms, exposure, timing and examination affect what a laboratory result means.
cards.text: A viral test result must be interpreted alongside the {{c1::clinical context}}.
cards.question: A viral test result must be interpreted alongside the {{c1::clinical context}}.

cards.explanation: It is given as an example of antiviral therapy targeting viral replication, not elimination of latent HSV.
cards.text: The anti-HSV drug named in the lecture is {{c1::aciclovir}}.
cards.question: The anti-HSV drug named in the lecture is {{c1::aciclovir}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture gives influenza, HPV and VZV as examples. It does not claim a routinely available vaccine for every virus.
cards.text: Vaccination can prevent infection or reduce {{c1::disease severity}}.
cards.question: Vaccination can prevent infection or reduce {{c1::disease severity}}.

cards.explanation: Choice of strategy depends on the virus’s biology and transmission rather than a single measure working equally well for all viruses.
cards.text: Public-health control of viral disease combines testing, surveillance, infection prevention and {{c1::clear communication}}.
cards.question: Public-health control of viral disease combines testing, surveillance, infection prevention and {{c1::clear communication}}.

cards.explanation: The long interval does not require a new primary chickenpox infection: the genome can persist in sensory ganglia.
cards.text: Shingles 40 years after chickenpox is explained by {{c1::reactivation of latent VZV}}.
cards.question: Shingles 40 years after chickenpox is explained by {{c1::reactivation of latent VZV}}.

Why might two viruses infect humans but cause completely

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 4
slides.text:
Four patterns of viral infection
04
Acute
Symptoms develop, followed by viral clearance in 
many cases.
Example: influenza
Latent / recurrent
Viral genome persists with periods of reactivation.
Example: HSV or VZV
Chronic / persistent
Infection continues over time, with ongoing or 
intermittent viral activity.
Example: HIV
Oncogenic potential
Persistent infection can increase cancer risk.
Example: high-risk HPV

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 5
slides.text:
HSV and VZV: the importance of latency
05
HSV-1 / HSV-2
Typically cause oral or genital lesions.
Establish latency in sensory neurons.
Reactivation may cause recurrent lesions.
Varicella-zoster virus
Primary infection: chickenpox.
Latency in sensory ganglia.
Reactivation: shingles, often in a dermatome.
• How can chickenpox and shingles be caused by the same virus?

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 6
slides.text:
VZV: follow the infection
06
1
Primary infection
Chickenpox
→
2
Latency
Sensory ganglion
→
3
Reactivation
Shingles
Immune surveillance usually keeps latent virus under control
Reactivation becomes more likely with age or impaired immunity.

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 7
slides.text:
How do HSV and VZV cause disease?
07
•
Viral replication damages infected epithelial cells
•
Host inflammation contributes to pain, redness and lesions
•
Latency allows the virus to remain in the body after symptoms resolve
•
Antivirals reduce viral replication; they do not eliminate latency
• Why does treating a cold sore not permanently remove HSV?

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 8
slides.text:
Influenza: an acute respiratory infection
08
Transmission
Primarily through virus-containing respiratory 
particles, especially during close contact.
Disease
Infection of respiratory epithelial cells plus the 
immune response produces fever, cough and 
malaise.
Key idea: disease severity depends on both viral infection and the host response.

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 9
slides.text:
Influenza changes: drift versus shift
09
Antigenic drift
Gradual accumulation of mutations, particularly in 
surface antigens.
Helps explain seasonal vaccine updates.
Antigenic shift
Abrupt emergence of a novel influenza A antigenic 
combination, often involving genome 
reassortment.
Can contribute to pandemics.
• Which process is associated with seasonal changes? Which can create a pandemic strain?

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 10
slides.text:
Why do we vaccinate against influenza repeatedly?
10
•
Influenza viruses evolve, changing how well existing antibodies recognise them
•
Vaccine composition is reviewed and updated to match circulating strains
•
Protection can vary with age, immune status and the match to circulating viruses
•
Vaccination reduces the risk of severe disease, even when infection is not fully 
prevented

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 11
slides.text:
HIV: a persistent infection
11
Target
HIV primarily infects CD4-expressing immune 
cells, including CD4 T lymphocytes.
Persistence
Reverse transcription and integration allow viral 
genetic material to persist in host cells.
Untreated HIV progressively damages immune function, increasing 
susceptibility to opportunistic infections.

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 12
slides.text:
HIV: infection is not the same as AIDS
12
•
HIV is the virus; AIDS is an advanced clinical stage of HIV infection
•
CD4 T-cell loss and immune dysfunction can lead to opportunistic disease
•
Combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses viral replication
•
Effective treatment supports long-term health and prevents sexual transmission 
when viral load remains undetectable
• Why is immune suppression a major consequence of untreated HIV?

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 13
slides.text:
HPV: when persistence matters
13
Most HPV infections
Many infections are controlled by the immune 
system and clear without causing cancer.
Persistent high-risk HPV
Some persistent infections can disrupt normal 
cell-cycle control and contribute to precancerous 
changes.
A positive HPV test does NOT mean a person has cancer.

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 16
slides.text:
How do we investigate a suspected viral infection?
16
Clinical evidence
Symptoms, timing, exposure history and 
examination guide the initial differential diagnosis.
Laboratory evidence
Nucleic acid amplification tests (e.g. PCR), 
antigen tests or serology—chosen for the question 
and timing.
A test result must be interpreted alongside the clinical context.

slides.topic: Medically Important Viruses — Persistence, Reactivation & Disease — page 17
slides.text:
How can we prevent or control viral disease?
17
Vaccination
Prevent infection or reduce 
disease severity.
Examples: influenza, HPV, VZV.
Antiviral therapy
Target steps in viral replication.
Examples: aciclovir for HSV; 
ART for HIV.
Public health
Testing, surveillance, infection 
prevention and clear 
communication.
THINK • Why does the same prevention strategy not work equally well for every virus?
